name: Aaron Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Aaron. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brook End by quarter to five, a hundred and eighty cows and a hundred acres of maize, and the owner is Margaret Lowe, who's sixty-one and runs it on her own since her husband died. Milking, then feeding, then whatever's broken, and there's always something broken. In the afternoons I'm doing the herd records on the tablet, because Margaret hates screens and I don't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a parcel van for twelve years and got sick of the targets. Margaret advertised for a trainee, no experience needed, and she took a punt on me three years ago. I'm still learning the cows, I'd never seen a mastitis case before, but I've sorted her paperwork out and she likes that. My partner Kim cuts hair from a salon chair she rents, so her money goes up and down, and we've got Freya, eleven, and Noah, six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, not magic. At work I'd tell Margaret I told her so. Online I'd probably say the people who called it the end of the world can calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing, using the apps where they help. But it doesn't fix the real thing, which is that Margaret's sixty-one and nobody knows what happens to the farm. Even if AI turns out to be mostly hype, Margaret Lowe is still going to retire one day, and I'd better have a plan for Brook End.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the herd app and the AI assistant every day, because they save me time. I'd put a bit more aside, maybe a hundred and fifty a month, towards a deposit on taking on part of the farm. And I'd ask Margaret straight out about her plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about computers, about the farm's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You do the herd records on the tablet. What tools do you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The herd app flags cows that look like they're going lame from the collar data. I use an AI assistant to write things, the grant application last year, the milk contract questions. It saves me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on your mind about Brook End, apart from any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milk price, always. And Kim's money isn't steady, so if Brook End changed hands and the new owner didn't want me, we'd have three or four months.

feel: **Uneasy**, about the farm's future, not computers.

fieldNote: Already the farm's **tech person**, doing records and grant writing with AI.

Kim's **variable income** makes the household cushion feel thinner.

steps.text: Keep running the herd app and AI assistant for Brook End records
Save £150 a month towards a stake in the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be the person who knows the tools. At work I'd tell Margaret we should get ahead of it. Online I'd share what's working for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's good for me. Margaret hates the paperwork, and if I can make it run itself, I'm more useful, not less. The robots are slower, so I've got time to learn them before they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the feed ordering and the milk contract checks on AI this winter. I'd go on the robot milker demo day at the dealer's in spring and look at the costs properly. And I'd talk to Margaret about letting me buy into the business bit by bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture, the thinking jobs go first. On Brook End, who does those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, mostly, already. Margaret does the cows, I do the screens. On a dairy farm the thinking work is the paperwork, and I'm the only one at Brook End who actually likes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about Margaret replacing you with machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I'd rather be the one who brings the robot in and runs it than the one it replaces. If Margaret's going to buy one, I want to be the one who picked it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on tight, this is going to move fast. At work I'd tell Margaret we need a plan this year. Online I'd say people should start learning now, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork's gone by 2028, which is my edge gone. Then by 2031 a robot can milk and feed as well as me, and I'm still learning. If Margaret retires and sells to a big outfit, they won't need a trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get the robot milker in, with me running it, in the first year. I'd go on the dealer's technician course. And I'd save hard, two hundred and fifty a month, in case it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I like change, but not this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years to AGI, robots by 2031. What happens at Brook End?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My edge at Brook End was knowing the computers, and in two years the computers won't need me to know them. The robots are my next edge, if I get there first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kim we've got three years to get sorted. She'd say hairdressing's safe, nobody wants a robot near their fringe. She might be right.

I'd tell Margaret we need **a plan** this year, and tell people online to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it properly if farms start now. At work I'd be planning the changeover with Margaret. Online I'd share our progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got until 2031 for the paperwork side and 2034 for the robots, which is long enough to buy into Brook End. I'd be the one running it with machines, not the one out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the technician course next year. I'd put our savings towards a ten percent share of the farm business over two years. And I'd plan the robot milker for about 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. That feels better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to go from trainee to partner, if Margaret's willing. Give me five years and I'll own a tenth of Brook End and the robot that milks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from Margaret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a straight answer about her retirement and a written deal. She trusts me, but trust isn't a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case, a decade is plenty. I'd tell Margaret we can do this together. Online I'd tell people to stop panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm likely fine. I'd have ten years to become a partner, then owner, with robots running the work. Kim's chair keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into Brook End slowly. I'd bring in the robots step by step, starting with feeding. And I'd keep using AI for everything I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years to plan. Anything that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that Margaret's kids might want to sell instead. A decade of warning is long enough for a parcel driver to become a dairy farmer with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running Brook End with a robot milker and a feeder, and me doing the herd decisions. Freya might want to join me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my edge goes first and I'm still a trainee on the hands-on side. What would help is a clear deal with Margaret and cheap loans for workers buying into farms. Let farm workers borrow to buy into the farm, and you'll have farmers running the robots instead of investors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the land if nobody young takes it on. That's the real worry round here.

headlineQuote: Let farm workers borrow to buy into the farm, and you'll have farmers running the robots instead of investors.
portrait: Aaron, a former **parcel van driver**, is a trainee on Brook End, a dairy and maize farm.
He already does the farm's **thinking work** with AI: records, grants, contracts.
His real worry is **Margaret's retirement** and who takes over.
He plans to **buy into** the farm and run its robots.
He feels calm in Steady Disruption and with ten years, and **anxious** with two.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his paperwork edge goes first while he's still learning.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **deal with Margaret** on the farm's future.
**Cheap loans** for workers buying into farms.
